Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Doing an Anti-PT will allow you to build control over your ability to apply the process when you intend to do so.

    • We can gain control over ourselves by seeing what happens when we purposefully turn control off.

  • Anti-PTs also have the opportunity to show you how good you really have become.

    • Plenty of advanced students are surprised by how well they do on an Anti-PT. Their process has become more subconscious than they realize.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: You can do an Accuracy Failsafe with any workout. Failsafes are time-training protocols that you can apply to any workout.

  1. Set your accuracy goal as a target number of wrong answers per section.

    1. An accuracy goal could be -5, for example.

  2. Complete an LR or RC section* at your natural pace.

  3. Take a five-minute break and Camo the section you just completed.

    1. If you have met your accuracy goal, proceed to a second section of the same type.

      1. This means if you just completed an RC section and hit your accuracy goal of -5, you would proceed to do another RC section with an accuracy goal of -5.

    2. If you have not met your accuracy goal on the first section, you have not beaten today's Failsafe.

      1. Do not decrease your target number of wrong answers tomorrow. Keep the same accuracy goal.

      2. Do not proceed to a second section of the same type today.

      3. Instead, Wrong Answer Journal and do one Recovery Workout (defined below) now.

  4. If you have proceeded to a second section, take a five-minute break and Camo it.

  5. If you have met your accuracy goal for the second time in a row, you have beaten today's Failsafe!

    1. Wrong Answer Journal both of today's sections.

    2. Decrease your target number of wrong answers tomorrow.

      1. This means that if you beat today's Failsafe of -5 accuracy, try for -4 accuracy on tomorrow's Failsafe.

  6. If you do not meet the accuracy goal on the second section, you have not beaten today's Failsafe.

    1. Wrong Answer Journal both of today's sections.

    2. Do not decrease your target number of wrong answers tomorrow. Keep the same accuracy goal.

  7. Return to Step 1 the following day.

Sections to use

New Sections Only

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Failsafes are a great Workout for the student who loves data and structured goals. 

  • Don't be intimidated by all the steps you see in the Failsafe.

    • Once you get into it, the flow of the Workout is relatively intuitive.

    • Essentially, if you meet your goals twice in a row, you move your goal. If you don't meet your goals twice in a row, you don't move your goal. 

  • Which Recovery Workout should you choose?

    • It depends on where you tend to feel difficulty throughout the section.

    • If you notice you miss questions from not translating the answer choices, going toward an Answer Choice Primer or MemAC could be a great move.

    • If you notice that you are making strategic mistakes, making a Highlight Reel is a safe bet. 

    • You can be the judge of which Recovery Workout is best for you, but the Recovery Workouts are designed to not allow you to simply repeat the exact same mistakes that you made in the first section of the FailSafe.

    • Even if you're tempted to go outside the list of Recovery Workout, don't do one that involves timed question answering.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage

What problem are we solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

  • you're falling asleep in the middle? 

  • someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

  • you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

  • you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

  • you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

  • you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
What Problem Are We Solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

you're falling asleep in the middle? 

someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

How you know you need to do this

Is this worth my time?

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

Remember the LR Full Question Process:

  1. Read and translate the stimulus in chunks. 

  2. Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

  3. Continue until end of stimulus.

  4. Mark the conclusion.

  5. Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

  6. Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

  7. Make a Mission.

    1. Making a Mission means answering the question yourself, except on Strengthen and Weaken questions. On these questions, your Mission should be a stimulus-specific goal for the answer choice to hit.

    2. You are allowed to go back to the stimulus when you make a Mission.

    3. Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

  8. On every individual answer choice:

    1. Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

    2. Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

      1. If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

      2. If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

      3. If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

  9. Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

  10. Hyperskip, if needed.

    1. Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

  11. Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

Accuracy
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
Prep Map
/
Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: An Analysis Skim is an addition to the RTQ stimulus process. You can seamlessly integrate it into any workout that involves an RTQ.

  1. Read, translate, and quip the stimulus well*.

  2. After you've quipped the last sentence of the stimulus, look at the whole stimulus again to take it apart and see what's really wrong.

    1. This is your Analysis Skim. This is not a moment to reread the stimulus from scratch and fix problems with your Translation.

    2. You must already have a solid memory of your Translation to perform an Analysis Skim.

    3. Ask yourself, "What's wrong with this?" while looking over the whole stimulus at once. This will make your Loophole textually based and provide an opportunity to mark the conclusion.

    4. Making your Loophole textual will enable you to critique the answers using mostly information from the stimulus instead of just information from the answers.

inline_prep.name: Stop Oversimplifying
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: You should not break up the individual Answer Choice Translation sections over more than one day, but completing the Answer Choice Primer in its entirety will take 6 prep days if you do one workout per day.

  1. For the first three days, complete new one section* per day of the Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet Drill (defined below), for a total of three Written sections.

  2. For the next three days, complete one new section per day of the Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drill (defined below), for a total of three Out Loud sections.

Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet Drills

  1. Make a spreadsheet with two columns, or use this template:

    1. Column 1: Answer Choice Text

    2. Column 2: Translation

  2. Read only the answer choices in the section.

    1. Do not read the stimulus.

    2. Do not read the question stem.

  3. Write down the text of each individual answer choice in the Answer Choice Text column.

    1. Do not copy/paste this text. Type the text yourself.

  4. Write down a Translation of each answer choice in the Translation column.

    1. This means read A, write the literal text of A, and write the Translation of A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E for each question.

    2. Your Translation of the answer choice cannot be a copy/paste of the answer choice text nor can it be exactly the same as the answer choice text. Translation means putting the same meaning in your own words.

Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drills

  1. Read only the answer choices in the section.

    1. Do not read the stimulus.

    2. Do not read the question stem.

  2. Translate the answer choice out loud.

  3. Quip the answer choice out loud.

    1. This means read A, translate A, and quip A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E for each question.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • The Answer Choice Translation Primer is responsible for bringing all the Translation skills you've built through your Translation + CLIR Drills into the answer choices.

    • This is such an important step to ensure consistent accuracy once we start answering questions.

    • Our standard of comprehension and retention must remain high throughout the entire question.

  • The Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet may be slow and difficult in the beginning.

    • Do not give up on this workout.

    • It gets much easier by the third section.

  • Keep your focus and commitment strong throughout the Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet portion of the Answer Choice Translation Primer.

    • Do not complete this Workout at a relaxed pace with frequent breaks.

    • Every interruption in the Workout decreases your pace of improvement.

  • If you're frequently taking longer than five minutes to complete one set of answer choices on the Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet, use a countdown timer to force yourself to finish each set of answer choices in five minutes or less.

  • Do not reuse the same sections for the Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet and Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drills.

  • Do not combine the Answer Choice Translation Primer with other Workouts.

inline_prep.name: Stop Oversimplifying
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

Accuracy
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
Prep Map

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

FIX 5 OF 7
Strengthen Your Working Memory
What Problem Are We Solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

How You Know You Need To Do This
Is This Worth My Time?
0
of
8

VERDICT:

No Idea, Really
You dread longer stimuli and answer choices
You blank out midway through questions even though you understood the stimulus
You find yourself having to "just pick something" because you forget what you're supposed to do
You rely on process of elimination because you can't remember the details clearly enough to identify the right answer
You ping-pong between your final two answers, constantly rereading them because they disappear from your memory immediately
You think your problem is "just the answer choices"
You rely heavily on looking back at the stimulus/passage in the answer choices
You re-read the same sentence multiple times hoping it will stick

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Open up a previously-seen LR or RC section*.

  2. Translate the first four questions' answer choices in the style of a Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet.

    1. Read only the answer choices for these four questions.

      1. Do not read the stimulus or the question stem.

    2. Write down each individual answer choice.

    3. Write down a Translation of each answer choice.

      1. This means read A, write the literal text of A, and write the Translation of A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.

    4. Use the same spreadsheet and same style as you used when you completed the Answer Choice Translation Primer.

  3. Translate the next four questions' answer choices in the style of an Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drill.

    1. Read only the answer choices in the section.

      1. Do not read the stimulus.

      2. Do not read the question stem.

    2. Translate the answer choice out loud.

    3. Quip the answer choice out loud.

      1. This means read A, translate A, and quip A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.

Sections to use

Ideal for Previously Seen Sections

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Grab a clean LR section* and start at question #1.

  2. Read the stimulus well once. You can go back and re-read sentences as you go, as much as you want. Once you hit the last period at the end of the stimulus, you’re done.

  3. Cover up the stimulus with your hand.

  4. In your head, say, “OK, so…” and tell yourself what happened in the stimulus. Do it casually, like you’re explaining a story to a friend.

  5. This explanation is your Translation of the stimulus. Write your Translation as a bulleted list in your notebook. Your goal is to reduce the stimulus to things that actually matter. By transforming the stimulus into your own words, you forget about the distracting jargon and focus more clearly.

  6. Read the stimulus again to see how close you were. Record where you were off base and why.

  7. Proceed to the next question and repeat these steps until you reach the end of the section. Do not read the question stem or answer choices on any of your Basic Translation Drills.

What problem are we solving?

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

  2. Take a few seconds to confirm your Translation with the paragraph you just read.

    1. In this step, you are not rereading from scratch. 

    2. You're confirming the Translation you already have is right. 

    3. This style of confirming your Translation with the text applies to every confirmation you ever do on RC.

  3. Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

  4. At the end of the passage, confirm your Translation with the entire passage. This should take 15-30 seconds.

  5. OPTIONAL: Look away and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of the entire passage silently.

    1. This step is optional, but you should do it when you first begin Caffeinated RC Translation Drills and periodically afterward, just to confirm that you can.

  6. Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

FIX 5 OF 7
Strengthen Your Working Memory
What Problem Are We Solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

How You Know You Need To Do This

You dread longer stimuli and answer choices
You blank out midway through questions even though you understood the stimulus

You rely on process of elimination because you can't remember the details clearly enough to identify the right answer
You ping-pong between your final two answers, constantly rereading them because they disappear from your memory immediately
You think your problem is "just the answer choices"
You rely heavily on looking back at the stimulus/passage in the answer choices
You re-read the same sentence multiple times hoping it will stick

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Timing Rules

    1. First Day:

      1. Do a Caffeinated Translation Drill on a passage with a stopwatch to establish your baseline natural pace*.

    2. All Other Days:

      1. Adopt the timing pattern that you earned the previous study day.

      2. Set a countdown timer for your baseline natural pace plus or minus the 20-second adjustment you have earned on your previous Failsafe.

  2. Read, translate, and quip the first paragraph silently.

  3. At the end of the paragraph, take a few seconds to relook at the paragraph and confirm that your Translation is right. Make sure you have everything and nothing is left out.

  4. Repeat the process on the subsequent paragraphs.

  5. At the end of the passage, take ~30 seconds or less to review the entire passage.

  6. Stop the time and write the time down.

  7. Off time, recap the Translation of the entire passage out loud. Check the text to see if there are any major gaps in your Translation. 

    1. If there are more than two gaps, you have not beaten the Failsafe. Increase the time by 20 seconds on your next Failsafe.

    2. If there are less than two gaps, you have beaten the Failsafe. Decrease the time by 20 seconds on your next Failsafe.

  8. You graduate from the Caffeinated RC Translation Drill Failsafes when you are able to beat the Failsafe consistently at an average of four minutes per passage while meeting theCaffeinated Translation Standard.

Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

    • Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

    • Taking breaks guarantees that the Translation Marathon will not work.

      • Do not check your phone.

      • Do not have conversations.

      • Do not take a lunch break.

    • Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

    • The only breaks allowed during Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

      • Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

      • Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

  • Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Translation Marathon.

  • Keep track of the order of the sections in your Translation Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

  • If you feel yourself getting worse as the Translation Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

    • This is not cause for alarm. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.

  • Set a section timer for 400 minutes in LawHub's Self-Paced Mode. Do not use Exam Mode.

  • Time each Caffeinated RC Translation Drill with an external stopwatch. Record the time each drill takes in your tracker.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. When you finish an LR or RC section in LawHub, do not press Complete Section. Instead, write down your answers.

    1. Use Self-Paced Mode on all LR and RC sections. Never use Exam Mode.

  2. At least 24 hours later, enter your answers into Camo Review.

    1. Do not check your answers against the answer key before entering your answers into Camo Review.

  3. Camo Review will give you a list of questions to return to.

    1. This list includes all of your wrong answers and an unknown number of decoy correct answers.

  4. Reattempt all of the questions in your Camo Review from scratch. Attempt to do a better job on the question now than you did the first time.

    1. Doing a better job means you should retranslate, requip, and re-CLIR the stimulus on LR or retranslate and requip the passage on RC. Retranslate every part of the question, consider every answer choice, and try to correct your process mistakes before choosing a new answer.

  5. Enter all your new answers into Camo Review.

  6. Camo Review will identify all your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, Self-Doubt, and Self-Confidence answers.

  7. Your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, and Self-Doubt answers have been automatically added to your Wrong Answer Journal. Go to your Wrong Answer Journal now to immediately begin the Wrong Answer Journal process.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Never Camo before doing your sections for the day. Always Camo as the last LSAT thing you do for the day.

    • If you Camo immediately before completing another section, you will be overly reactive to the result.

    • If the previous day's section went well, this can make you lazy.

    • If it went poorly, this can make you discouraged.

    • It's not worth taking the risk of either of these reactions affecting your performance on the next section.

  • The only point of Camo Review is to get a -0.

    • Do not phone in the Camo Review or rechoose the answer you originally chose out of loyalty because you aren't sure it's wrong.

    • If you got more than two questions back in the Camo Review, some of the questions are definitely wrong, so you must change at least some of them.

  • Do not Camo a section immediately after completing it, unless you are directed explicitly to do so as part of another Workout or Routine.

    • If you Camo a section immediately after completing it, the Camo score will be worse and you will lose a valuable opportunity to improve.

Previously Seen Sections Only

HOW TO TIME

Untimed

Ellen's Advice
If You Want to Win

Never Camo before doing your sections for the day. Always Camo as the last LSAT thing you do for the day.

If you Camo immediately before completing another section, you will be overly reactive to the result.

If the previous day's section went well, this can make you lazy.

If it went poorly, this can make you discouraged.

It's not worth taking the risk of either of these reactions affecting your performance on the next section.

The only point of Camo Review is to get a -0.

Do not phone in the Camo Review or rechoose the answer you originally chose out of loyalty because you aren't sure it's wrong.

If you got more than two questions back in the Camo Review, some of the questions are definitely wrong, so you must change at least some of them.

Do not Camo a section immediately after completing it, unless you are directed explicitly to do so as part of another Workout or Routine.

If you Camo a section immediately after completing it, the Camo score will be worse and you will lose a valuable opportunity to improve.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: Cappuccino is similar to Decaf, except instead of recapping all of your Translations after finishing with each paragraph, you’ll be looking back at the text to confirm your Translations.

  1. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

  2. Look away from paragraph 1 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 1 silently.

  3. Take a few seconds to confirm your Translation with the paragraph you just read.

    1. In this step, you are not rereading from scratch. 

    2. You're confirming the Translation you already have is right.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Read, translate, and quip every sentence*. Max every two sentences if they are really simple. Exactly how you would translate in LR. 

  2. At the end of each paragraph, pause to review the Translation while looking at the paragraph and confirm with yourself that you really know it. 

    1. In this step, you are not rereading from scratch. 

    2. You're confirming the Translation you already have is right. 

    3. This style of confirming your Translation with the text applies to every confirmation you ever do on RC.

  3. After each paragraph, relook at all the paragraphs that you've read so far to confirm they are placed in your memory. 

  4. Continue on until the end of the passage with the same process.

  5. At the end of the passage, do a final review by relooking at the entire passage and reconfirming your Translation. This should take about 30 seconds.

  6. Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

    • Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

    • Taking breaks guarantees that the Marathon will not work.

      • Do not check your phone.

      • Do not have conversations.

      • Do not take a lunch break.

    • Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

    • The only breaks allowed during Translation Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

      • Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

      • Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

  • Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Translation Marathon.

  • Keep track of the order of the sections in your Translation Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

  • If you feel yourself getting worse as the Translation Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

    • This is not cause for alarm. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.

Timing Tips

  • Set a section timer for 400 minutes in LawHub's Self-Paced Mode. Do not use Exam Mode.

  • Time each Cappuccino RC Translation Drill with an external stopwatch. Record the time each drill takes in your tracker.

Quick Facts
Will This Help Me?

THIS WILL HELP YOU IF

You need to reduce your Cappuccino RC Translation time while retaining a high standard of passage retention.

SKIP FOR NOW IF

You cannot accurately recap the entire passage at the end of a Cappuccino RC Translation Drill.

CHALLENGE INDEX
Ellen Whyyy
LEVEL
Beginner
MINIMUM TIME
144+ minutes
TIMING COMPATIBLE WITH
Stopwatch
Instructions
Complete six to eight Cappuccino RC Translation Drills* in one sitting with no breaks.

SECTIONS TO USE

Mix in Previously Seen Sections

HOW TO TIME

Count-Up Stopwatch

Ellen's Advice
If You Want to Win

It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

Taking breaks guarantees that the Marathon will not work.

Do not check your phone.

Do not have conversations.

Do not take a lunch break.

Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

The only breaks allowed during Translation Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Translation Marathon.

Keep track of the order of the sections in your Translation Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

If you feel yourself getting worse as the Translation Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

This is not cause for alarm. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.
SHOW LESS
Timing Tips

Set a section timer for 400 minutes in LawHub's Self-Paced Mode. Do not use Exam Mode.

Time each Cappuccino RC Translation Drill with an external stopwatch. Record the time each drill takes in your tracker.

inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

FIX 4 OF 7
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
What Problem Are We Solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
What Problem Are We Solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Instructions

NOTE: Do your recaps out loud in the beginning to keep yourself honest about the quality and completeness of the recaps. Transition to silent recaps when you feel like you're ready.

  1. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

    1. This means all the details are included just like they would be on LR.

    2. Quip after every Translation. 

    3. This standard applies to every paragraph you ever translate on RC.

  2. Look away from paragraph 1 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 1 silently.

    1. The recap is not a summary, gist, or main point.

    2. The recap should not omit names, dates, and lists.

    3. The recap should not be a shopping list of information. It should be a story in your own words.

    4. It is encouraged to mix up the order of the sentences and ideas.

    5. This standard applies to every paragraph (or collection of paragraphs) you ever recap on RC.

  3. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 2. Do it just like LR.

  4. Look away from paragraph 2 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 2 silently.

  5. Without looking back, recap the Translations of paragraphs 1 + 2 back to back silently.

  6. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 3. Do it just like LR.

  7. Look away from paragraph 3 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 3 silently.

  8. Without looking back, recap the Translations of paragraphs 1 + 2 + 3 back to back silently.

  9. Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

  10. Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

NOTE: Do your recaps out loud in the beginning to keep yourself honest about the quality and completeness of the recaps. Transition to silent recaps when you feel like you're ready.

Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

This means all the details are included just like they would be on LR.

Quip after every Translation. 

This standard applies to every paragraph you ever translate on RC.

Look away from paragraph 1 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 1 silently.

The recap is not a summary, gist, or main point.

The recap should not omit names, dates, and lists.

The recap should not be a shopping list of information. It should be a story in your own words.

It is encouraged to mix up the order of the sentences and ideas.

This standard applies to every paragraph (or collection of paragraphs) you ever recap on RC.

Look away from paragraph 2 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 2 silently.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.
