And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

    • Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

    • Taking breaks guarantees that the Marathon will not work.

      • Do not check your phone.

      • Do not have conversations.

      • Do not take a lunch break.

    • Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

    • The only breaks allowed during Translation Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

      • Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

      • Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

  • Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Translation Marathon.

  • Keep track of the order of the sections in your Translation Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

  • If you feel yourself getting worse as the Translation Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

    • This is not cause for alarm. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.

Timing Tips

  • Set a section timer for 400 minutes in LawHub's Self-Paced Mode. Do not use Exam Mode.

  • Time each Decaf RC Translation Drill with an external stopwatch. Record the time each drill takes in your tracker.

    2. The Low Density column is where you write your low information density Missions.

      1. A Mission with low information density will use referential phrasing ("this," "that," "it," "they," "the conclusion," etc.) to gloss over the direct words and concepts from the stimulus, omit the details like specific nouns and verbs, and group information together with broad characterizations ("good things").

      2. Example Mission on the Same Question in the Low-Density Bucket: Food is important

  5. Return to the questions that produced Low-Density Missions the next day and try to make a new higher density Mission before you Camo the section.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • E Blackouts are the single best answer choice analysis training workout around.

  • E Blackouts one of the only effective ways I've found to stop Early Answer Lock In and E Bias. No other workout even comes close.

  • E Blackouts force you to stop choosing answer comparatively.

    • On an E Blackout, you can't scan every answer and select the "best answer" by process of elimination.

    • You are forced to gauge each answer's individual relationship to the stimulus using the Back Up Plan, which results in much higher accuracy.

  • E Blackouts look a lot scarier than they actually are. Give them a chance, and you'll see that they make you a better test taker.

    • Weird but a lot of students improve their score when they E Blackout.

  • I know you might not believe me, but a tutoring student did E Blackout their real LSAT and got a 180. I have the receipts.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

FIX 4 OF 7
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
What Problem Are We Solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Every day, translate elevated reading material from outside the LSAT, using the following sources:

    1. ScienceDaily.com

      1. Ideal daily reading for those who feel alienated by scientific language or fear science passages in RC

      2. Be sure to choose the articles that challenge you the most, not articles that look familiar or interesting

    2. Aeon.co

      1. The most similar articles to LSAT RC on the internet

      2. Reading an Aeon.co article every day is a great habit if you have no specific topic-based weaknesses, but would like to make RC-style reading a habit.

    3. ALDaily.com

      1. Ideal daily reading for those who feel alienated by abstract language, art, humanities, and pretension.

      2. Be sure to choose the articles that look the most unfamiliar, not articles that speak to your pre-existing interests.

    4. NYT Guide to Essential Knowledge

      1. The single best way to fix gaps in common knowledge

      2. Here is a list of sections in the Guide that are relevant to LSAT. If any of these topics would trouble you as an RC passage, read over that section of the guide.

      3. LSAT Relevant Guide Sections: Architecture, Zoology, Botany, History, Art, Photography, Literature, Music (the serious parts about jazz and blues, especially), Film, Dance, Drama, Climate & Weather and Glossary of Weather Words (In Geography), Government, Law, Philosophy, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Astronomy, Geology

    5. Crash Course

      1. Not a written source, but Crash Course is too useful for solving common knowledge gaps to not include

      2. Watch Crash Course while you're in line, waiting for someone, on hold, brushing your teeth, etc. Any time you could be scrolling on your phone, watch Crash Course instead.

      3. Top Five LSAT Relevant Crash Course Sections: Intellectual Property (Ellen's favorite for LSAT students), Economics, US Government & Politics, Art History, and Philosophy

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

Our goal is threefold:

  • Expand your vocabulary

    • Harvest challenging words from your extracurricular reading and add it to them to your Vocab Tracker.

    • Practice these new words daily with or without AI.

  • Familiarize you with new academic topics

    • Many student have trouble locking in on topics that they find boring or unfamiliar. Expand your common knowledge so there are fewer topics that shake you.

    • Always choose topics that you are least familiar with and least interested in.  

  • Improve your Translation skills

    • Your Translation skill set is one of the primary determinants of your test-day performance, but real LSAT material is limited.

    • By translating outside sources, you get the chance to improve your Translation skill without only relying on non-renewable LSAT materials.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

    • Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

    • Taking breaks guarantees that the Marathon will not work.

      • Do not check your phone.

      • Do not have conversations.

      • Do not take a lunch break.

    • Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

    • The only breaks allowed during Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

      • Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

      • Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

  • Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Marathon.

  • It is exceptionally important that you do not see the score of each section in the middle of the Marathon.

    • If you see the scores, it will take out of the focused activity and all the intuition-building work will be undone. The Marathon will be wasted.

  • Marathons should be performed on only one type of section at a time unless otherwise specified (as in, Mixed Section Marathons).

    • This means that all the sections of the Marathon are LR, or all the sections of the Marathon are RC.

  • Keep track of the order of the sections in your Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

  • If you feel yourself getting worse as the Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

    • This is ok, but it indicates that you’ll need to do another Marathon. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.

  • At the end of the Marathon, take a break and then Camo all the sections in a big batch.

Timing Tips

The timing protocols for your Failsafe Marathon will be determined by the Timing Failsafe instructions. There are plenty of details there on exactly how you should time each section.

inline_prep.html:

Failsafe Marathon Routine
  1. Prep Map/

Failsafe Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

Failsafe Marathon Routines combine the best of Failsafes with the best of Marathons.

These Routines can be brutal, especially if you don't beat the Failsafe frequently. But the same thing that makes them punishing also makes them effective.

They're a blunt instrument that will change you as a test taker, so they are often relied upon in emergency situations.

When a test date is within one week and you still aren't able to complete the section in time with goal-level accuracy, this is your Routine.

LR
RC

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

How to Pull This Off

Failsafe Marathons Routines work well to speed up the progress of a Failsafe Routine.

Sometimes, students will see a lot of traction with Failsafes, but the pace of bringing the time down little by little each day can feel limiting, especially with a near-term test date.

Failsafe Marathon Routines are like the "In Case of Emergency Break the Glass" of the Prep Map.

They are harsh, but they will push you harder than almost any other workout.

How to move on

If you have lost every Failsafe you've attempted in your Failsafe Marathon for three consecutive prep days, here are a few options for what you can try next:

  1. Set a higher baseline natural pace to start your Failsafe Marathon

  2. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with a Light Failsafe

  3. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with Pacing Practice

  4. Return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

If you sometimes hit goal time and accuracy in your Failsafe Marathon, progress to any of the following Speed Routines: Marathon Routine, Mixed Timing Marathon Routine, or Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine. 

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Failsafe Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Practice Occurs Under Full Test Conditions

What problem are we solving?

You should not take an official LSAT until you have practiced regularly in test conditions. This means you're practicing in a quiet environment, taking exactly the allocated time you'll have on test day (no more no less), and you are not taking breaks to go on your phone or talk to people. Practicing in chaotic, unplanned conditions causes more score chaos than you'd think.

sections.html:
Real Examples

170+ Scorer LR Highlight Reel

  • Please be consistent in how I approach the questions (BTD & CLIR). I am doing myself a disservice by straying from the right approach.

  • Read all answer choices thoroughly

  • "At least as quickly or as many as another" means greater than or equal to. Remember that there is a middle ground of being equal in number/characteristic

  • Don't make the right loophole and then choose an answer choice that doesn't match my loophole

  • Don't make the right loophole and then freak out when none of the answer choices match my loophole. The LSAT will say your loophole in different (more convoluted) language

  • The answer lies in the stimulus. If you are stuck on a question because none of the answer choices seem right then go back to the stimulus first and re-read MORE CAREFULLY instead of doing a cursory read of the stimulus and judging between the answer choices or digging yourself into a hole. Lower the bar that you've set for what needs to be in the right answer choice.

  • Don't pick an answer choice if you know that something is not quite 100% with it. Even if you've dismissed the other ACs maybe you dismissed it too fast.

  • Read words on the LSAT literally. Be sensitive to the meaning of words.

170+ Scorer RC Highlight Reel

  • Don't help out answer choices:

    • The correct answer finds support in the passage

    • Don't mold the more obviously wrong answer choice into the correct answer. You probably missed something that made you dismiss the correct answer choice too quickly

  • Come up with a Mission before diving into the answer choices every time

  • Keep in mind RC answer choices will mesh different ideas together. Remember why and where the author talks about different concepts.

  • Read answer choices carefully: for example clauses that qualify a noun (ex. Western church boards THAT sent the greatest number of women missionaries)

  • Don't miss the forest for the trees: Don't just keyword words like "most". Ask yourself what this answer choice is saying as a whole as well

  • If you are debating between answer choices, and you know that neither is quite right, then STOP and re-evaluate the other answers

inline_prep.name: Learn From Your Mistakes
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

FIX 3 OF 7
Learn From Your Mistakes

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 3 OF 7
Learn From Your Mistakes
What Problem Are We Solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

How You Know You Need To Do This
Is This Worth My Time?

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: Do not attempt HIIT if you have never done a Thunderdome. Ideally, you've done several Thunderdomes and begun to feel confident while Thunderdoming before ever attempting HIIT.

  1. After you finish your Translation + CLIR on a given stimulus at 20-minute pace, complete the stimulus' Thunderdome without looking at the stimulus again*.

  2. Cap each Thunderdome output at 30 seconds outloud.

    1. Use AI voice dictation to record your Thunderdome outputs while keeping the workout speedy. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

  3. If you go over 30 seconds per Thunderdome output, don't worry about it. Just aiming for 30 seconds will make you faster.

Ideal for Previously Seen Sections

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is not important to look at the question stem and answer choices during a HIIT.

    • The point of this workout is not to answer questions, but if you want to combine it with answer-choosing, I'm not fully against it.

  • Don't attempt to HIIT as a beginner.

    • If you haven't met the Translation time goal or don't have significant experience with full LR sections, wait to HIIT until you need it.

  • For the right kind of plateaued, advanced test taker, HIIT offer a singular opportunity for a perspective shift.

  • HIITs show you where you're weak.

    • If you find that you always struggle with one of the HIIT outputs, review the videos and written material on that topic.

  • HIITs are great for when you start to run out of unseen PTs near the end of your prep.

    • HIITs can still be done on previously seen material.

  • If you are an advanced student PTing at 172+, HIITing can really take your skills to the next level.

  • Like Translation + CLIR Drills, HIITs are a great spot to use AI voice dictation to speed up the workout. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

Instructions

  1. Before starting your section*, draw the following two-column chart on your scratch paper, or use this template:

    1. Column 1 Header: Original answer is WRONG

    2. Column 2 Header: New answer is CORRECT

    3. Draw horizontal lines below the header to represent rows in the chart.

  2. As you complete the section, write the number of each hyperskipped question on the left side of each row.

    1. When you return to each hyperskipped question on the hyperskip pass, investigate whether you meet:

      1. The "Original answer is WRONG" criterion

      2. The "New answer is CORRECT" criterion

  3. If you meet each criterion, check the appropriate column in the row for that question.

  4. If you check both columns on a question, you can change your answer.

    1. This means you met both criteria for that question.

  5. If you do not have two checkmarks on a question within 90 seconds of returning to the question, you cannot change your answer.

inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

TELL ELLEN
FIX 4 OF 7
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
What Problem Are We Solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Instructions

  1. OPTIONAL: Read the first and last sentence of the passage.

    1. Translate and quip these sentences. Add the sentences up to get an idea of what the passage is likely about.

    2. These sentences should allow you to think inferentially, not just limit your Party Tricking to what was literally mentioned in the first and last sentence.

  2. Party Trick the passage's questions.

    1. Write down your answers so you know your Party Trick accuracy later, even if you change your answer after reading the passage.

  3. RC Translation Drill the passage.

    1. Whether you use Decaf, Cappuccino, or Caffeinated depends on where you are in your prep, so use whichever one you're currently on.

  4. Re-attempt the questions.

  5. Repeat this process on all the remaining passages in the section*.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage

What problem are we solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

  • you're falling asleep in the middle? 

  • someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

  • you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

  • you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

  • you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

  • you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

Is this worth my time?

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: You can do a Light Failsafe with any workout. Failsafes are time-training protocols that you can apply to any workout.

  1. Timing Rules

    1. First Day: Do a stopwatch-timed section* to establish your baseline natural pace.

    2. All Other Days: Adopt the timing pattern that you earned previously. Use a countdown timer for section timing once you have begun to lower your time goal.

Timing Failsafe Routine

Why are we doing this?

Timing Failsafe Routines are one of the only ways to effectively reduce time without Marathoning.

The upsides of Timing Failsafes are:

  • They can be done in shorter periods of time than a Marathon

  • They allow for more systematic gradual time reduction

  • Review can be more targeted and frequent

This Routine works great for students who thrive on structure.

How to Pull This Off

Failsafe Routines work best when combined with other Routines to bring time down while maintaining accuracy.

Essentially, you have to address the reasons why the Failsafe breaks in order to get it to progress, so you'll want to consider alternating Failsafe Routines with the Accuracy Fix Routines that pertain to your mistakes.

How to move on

Timing Failsafe Routines can get you to test-day goal time and accuracy without progressing to any other Speed Routine.

However, if you have lost every Timing Failsafe you've attempted for three consecutive prep days, here are a few options for what you can try next:

  1. Set a higher baseline natural pace to start your Timing Failsafe

  2. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with a Light Failsafe

  3. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with Pacing Practice

  4. Return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

If you sometimes hit goal time and accuracy in your Timing Failsafes, progress to any of the following Speed Routines: Failsafe Marathon Routine, Mini-Marathon Routine, or Marathon Routine.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Timing Failsafe Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage

What problem are we solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

  • you're falling asleep in the middle? 

  • someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

  • you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

  • you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

  • you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

  • you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
What Problem Are We Solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

you're falling asleep in the middle? 

someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

  1. Prep Map/

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Practice Occurs Under Full Test Conditions

What problem are we solving?

You should not take an official LSAT until you have practiced regularly in test conditions. This means you're practicing in a quiet environment, taking exactly the allocated time you'll have on test day (no more no less), and you are not taking breaks to go on your phone or talk to people. Practicing in chaotic, unplanned conditions causes more score chaos than you'd think.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Read and translate the stimulus in chunks*. 

  2. Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

  3. Continue until the end of the stimulus.

  4. Mark the conclusion.

  5. Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

  6. Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

  7. Make a Mission.

    1. Making a Mission means answering the question yourself, except on Strengthen and Weaken questions. On these questions, your Mission should be a stimulus-specific goal for the answer choice to hit.

    2. You are allowed to go back to the stimulus when you make a Mission.

    3. Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

  8. On every individual answer choice:

    1. Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

    2. Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

      1. If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

      2. If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

      3. If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

  9. Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

  10. Hyperskip, if needed.

    1. Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

  11. Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

    • Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

    • Taking breaks guarantees that the Marathon will not work.

      • Do not check your phone.

      • Do not have conversations.

      • Do not take a lunch break.

    • Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

    • The only breaks allowed during Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

      • Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

      • Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

  • Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Marathon.

  • It is exceptionally important that you do not see the score of each section in the middle of the Marathon.

    • If you see the scores, it will take out of the focused activity and all the intuition-building work will be undone. The Marathon will be wasted.

  • Marathons should be performed on only one type of section at a time unless otherwise specified (as in, Mixed Section Marathons).

    • This means that all the sections of the Marathon are LR, or all the sections of the Marathon are RC.

  • Keep track of the order of the sections in your Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

  • If you feel yourself getting worse as the Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

    • This is ok, but it indicates that you’ll need to do another Marathon. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.

  • At the end of the Marathon, take a break and then Camo all the sections in a big batch.

Timing Tips

How Marathon Timing Works

  • Use a stopwatch and a 35-minute countdown timer on LawHub to time your sections.

    • In LawHub, use Self-Paced Mode. Do not use Exam Mode.

    • If you have extended time, change the 35-minute countdown timer to the amount of time you have to complete the section according to your accommodations.

  • If the countdown timer runs out and you are not done, write down what question you were on when time ran out. Continue the section until you finish, and write down the time it took you to finish as soon as you finish it.

    • Just look down at the stopwatch when you finish it and write down what you see.

  • Keep track of the timed and untimed score after you review.

  • Do not pretend that Marathon timing is the same as test-day timing.

    • Do not do all the Marathon sections with bad form in order to meet test-day timing before you're ready. It is expected that you first few Marathons will contain sections that go far beyond the test-day time limit.

    • Pretending that you're ready for test-day timed sections before you're actually ready for them (finishing Marathons within the test-day time limit even though this deeply hurts your accuracy) will only ingrain bad form and make you significantly worse. I don't want to hurt you, so PLEASE do not do this. Let the Marathon sections take longer than test-day timed sections, if they need to in order to maintain the accuracy.

  • If you are consistently finishing your Marathon sections within 35 minutes (or 36/37 minutes) and your accuracy is suffering, do your Marathons with a stopwatch only and no countdown timer. Set LawHub to 400 minutes at the start of each section so the timer doesn't bother you.

inline_prep.name: Marathon Routine
inline_prep.html:
Speed
Marathon Routine
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Speed

Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

The Marathon Routine is the most effective Routine in the Prep Map for pure speed improvement.

No other Routine or workout will increase speed like this Routine.

The purpose of the Marathon Routine is to decrease the time it takes to get questions right by exhausting you to the point where your subconscious intuition will have to kick in to complete the questions.

This Routine will eventually enable you to finish the section in time at goal accuracy.

LR
RC
FrequencySpaced Set
Challenge IndexEllen Whyyy
LevelAdvanced
Study block4-5+ hours
Time goal to move on20 min

Routine Schedule

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

1

The Island

10 minutes
2

Translation + CLIR Drill

1 section
3

Marathon

8 sections
4

Camo Review

5

Wrong Answer Journal

How to Pull This Off

Marathons have a ton of specific, crucial instructions, so make sure you internalize the Marathon timing procedures, section data to track, and advice on how to win contained in the Marathon Workout instructions.

When adding Marathon Routines to your prep, be strategic about section usage.

Since one Marathon uses several PTs, you have to stay mindful about your consumption of these non-renewable resources. It can be advisable to mix previously-seen material into some Marathons to minimize material usage.

Make sure you don't Marathon all the most recent PTs; this will leave you with no fresh exams to use as full test-conditions practice tests.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

Marathon Routines can get you to test-day goal time and accuracy without progressing to any other Speed Routine.

However, you should change your Speed Routine, if you notice any of the following issues in your Marathon Routine:

  1. Your speed and accuracy on new sections have plateaued or gotten worse for three Marathons in a row

    1. Try a Timing Failsafe Routine or return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

  2. You don't have uninterrupted blocks of time on your calendar for Marathons and you are unwilling to adjust your calendar

    1. Move to a Timing Failsafe Routine

  3. Your score decreases when you switch from LR to RC or RC to LR

    1. Move to a Mixed Section Marathon Routine

If you're still not hitting your time and accuracy goals, or you're just starting to reach your time goals while maintaining accuracy on a few sections, you probably need to do more Marathon Routines.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Marathon Routine
Why Are We Doing This?

The Marathon Routine is the most effective Routine in the Prep Map for pure speed improvement.

No other Routine or workout will increase speed like this Routine.

The purpose of the Marathon Routine is to decrease the time it takes to get questions right by exhausting you to the point where your subconscious intuition will have to kick in to complete the questions.

This Routine will eventually enable you to finish the section in time at goal accuracy.

Routine Schedule

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

1
The Island

How To Pull This Off

Marathons have a ton of specific, crucial instructions, so make sure you internalize the Marathon timing procedures, section data to track, and advice on how to win contained in the Marathon Workout instructions.

When adding Marathon Routines to your prep, be strategic about section usage.

Since one Marathon uses several PTs, you have to stay mindful about your consumption of these non-renewable resources. It can be advisable to mix previously-seen material into some Marathons to minimize material usage.

Make sure you don't Marathon all the most recent PTs; this will leave you with no fresh exams to use as full test-conditions practice tests.

Marathon Routine Protocols

Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How To Move On

Marathon Routines can get you to test-day goal time and accuracy without progressing to any other Speed Routine.

However, you should change your Speed Routine, if you notice any of the following issues in your Marathon Routine:

Your speed and accuracy on new sections have plateaued or gotten worse for three Marathons in a row

Try a Timing Failsafe Routine or return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

You don't have uninterrupted blocks of time on your calendar for Marathons and you are unwilling to adjust your calendar

Move to a Timing Failsafe Routine

Your score decreases when you switch from LR to RC or RC to LR

Move to a Mixed Section Marathon Routine

If you're still not hitting your time and accuracy goals, or you're just starting to reach your time goals while maintaining accuracy on a few sections, you probably need to do more Marathon Routines.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Masterpiece

Perfect one section over multiple days to fix the deepest accuracy issues

Deep Accuracy Fix
RC/LR
Accuracy

Quick Facts

Will This Help Me?

This will help you if

You have persistent, difficult-to-fix accuracy problems and you have been at an undesirable accuracy level for a long time. Masterpieces are the break-in-case-of-emergency accuracy fix drill.

Skip for now if

You don't have serious accuracy problems.

challenge indexBuckle Up
levelIntermediate
minimum time60+ minutes
timing compatible withNatural Pace

Instructions

NOTE: Masterpieces are multi-day workouts focused on a single section*. You can do a three-day Masterpiece or a four-day Masterpiece to start. Don't worry, you do less and less work as the Masterpiece progresses each day.

  1. Complete the section in any workout style.

    1. Mark questions for hyperskip, but don't perform your hyperskip pass yet.

    2. When you're done with the section, put it aside without grading it.

  2. The next day, redo each question in the section fully.

    1. When you return to the section, keep your answer selected at first, but uncross off all other answer choices.

    2. Do not just look at your previous answer without actually redoing the full question. Your objective is to decide whether you want to stick to your previous answer or choose a new answer.

    3. On each question you have three options:

      1. Lock in your previous answer.

        1. Once an answer is locked, you will not look at this question again until Camo Day. Locking is a way to signal to yourself that you know this answer is correct and do not need to look at it again.

        2. Do not lock in more than 50% of your remaining answers on any lock-in pass until you get to the last day of your Masterpiece.

      2. Keep your answer the same, but leave the question unlocked.

        1. Leave a question unlocked if you are not sure about whether the answer you've selected is correct.

      3. Change your answer.

        1. If you change your answer, you may not lock the question on this pass.

  3. The next day, return only to your unlocked questions and redo them. Decide to lock in or change your answers, following the same procedure you did on day 2.

    1. This process repeats for however many days your Masterpiece will last.

    2. Make sure all questions are locked in by the last day.

  4. Optional: On the last day, print out a fresh copy of the section and redo it straight-through.

    1. Compare the fresh section to your locked-in answers and see if there are any differences. If so, reconcile the two sections. Decide on your final answer before putting it into Camo.

  5. After your last pass on the section, with all answers locked in, proceed with Camo and Wrong Answer Journaling.

New Sections Only

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: MemAC is a multi-day series of workouts using previously-seen LR and RC sections that progress through five levels as you meet certain benchmarks. Each level and benchmark is defined below. MemAC can be completed as a full section* or by completing as much MemAC as possible in 1-3 hour blocks.

  1. Start MemAC at Level 1, or from wherever you left off previously.

    1. Level 1 MemAC means that you will be performing the answer choice Translation process defined in the Level 1 instructions below. If you are on a later Level, follow the corresponding instructions below.

  2. To Level Up: Complete the full MemAC process defined in your Level instructions without having to peek at the answer choices to accurately remember them on 10 questions in a row.

    1. For example, if you correctly recap all the answer choices on 10 questions in a row without having to peek on Level 1, move to Level 2 on the next question.

  3. Each time you complete one full section of MemAC, complete a MemAC Live Check-In Question(defined below).

MemAC Live Check-In Question

  1. Complete a full LR question according to the Full LR Process. 

    1. Just translate and quip the answers normally. Do not do MemAC.

  2. After choosing your answer, attempt to translate all the answer choices from memory. 

  3. Write down how many answers you're able to translate from memory on each Live Check-In Question.

  4. Compare the number of answers you're able to translate from memory across all your Live Check-In Questions to measure your progress.

MemAC Level 1: One answer at a time

When you beat Level 1, progress to Level 2.

  1. Read, translate, and quip answer choice A.

  2. Repeat the Translation of A from memory.

  3. Read, translate, and quip answer choice B.

  4. Repeat the Translation of A and B from memory.

  5. Read, translate, and quip answer choice C.

  6. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C from memory.

  7. Read, translate, and quip answer choice D.

  8. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D from memory.

  9. Read, translate, and quip answer choice E.

  10. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D, E from memory.

MemAC Level 2: Two answers at a time

When you beat Level 2, progress to Level 3.

  1. Read, translate, and quip answer choice A.

  2. Read, translate, and quip answer choice B.

  3. Repeat the Translation of A and B from memory.

  4. Read, translate, and quip answer choice C.

  5. Read, translate, and quip answer choice D.

  6. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D from memory.

  7. Read, translate, and quip answer choice E.

  8. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D, E from memory.

MemAC Level 3: Three answers at a time

When you beat Level 3, progress to Level 4.

  1. Read, translate, and quip answer choice A.

  2. Read, translate, and quip answer choice B.

  3. Read, translate, and quip answer choice C.

  4. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C from memory.

  5. Read, translate, and quip answer choice D.

  6. Read, translate, and quip answer choice E.

  7. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D, E from memory.

MemAC Level 4: Four answers at a time

When you beat Level 4, progress to Level 5.

  1. Read, translate, and quip answer choice A.

  2. Read, translate, and quip answer choice B.

  3. Read, translate, and quip answer choice C.

  4. Read, translate, and quip answer choice D.

  5. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D from memory.

  6. Read, translate, and quip answer choice E.

  7. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D, E from memory.

MemAC Level 5: Five answers at a time

When you beat Level 5, congratulations! You've beaten MemAC!

  1. Read, translate, and quip answer choice A.

  2. Read, translate, and quip answer choice B.

  3. Read, translate, and quip answer choice C.

  4. Read, translate, and quip answer choice D.

  5. Read, translate, and quip answer choice E.

  6. Repeat the Translation of A, B, C, D, E from memory.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Don't halfway commit to doing MemAC. The first few hours are by far the most stressful and slow. Do not give up. There is so much benefit on the other side.

  • Do not read the stimulus or question stem during MemAC.

  • Do not Party Trick the answer choices during MemAC.

  • Many students move MemAC to a warmup after they beat Level 5.

    • They report that they feel like they're at peak mental clarity when they're MemACing.

  • MemAC is the midpoint of answer choice mastery.

    • Typically, I'll have my students complete the Answer Choice Primer, then MemAC, then Party Tricking.

    • After you beat Level 5 of MemAC, consider trying out Party Tricking Jail.

  • If you're currently missing more than 10 questions per LR or RC questions, brace yourself that MemAC will be difficult and you will have to work hard to improve your skills. Do not let this difficulty dissuade you from investing in the workout.

Timing Tips

  • Beginner students complete 6 MemAC questions per hour 

  • Intermediate students complete 12 MemAC questions per hour

  • Advanced students complete 20 MemAC questions per hour 

  • Expert students complete a whole section of MemAC in an hour

Instructions

NOTE: MemAC is a multi-day series of workouts using previously-seen LR and RC sections that progress through five levels as you meet certain benchmarks. Each level and benchmark is defined below. MemAC can be completed as a full section* or by completing as much MemAC as possible in 1-3 hour blocks.

Start MemAC at Level 1, or from wherever you left off previously.

Level 1 MemAC means that you will be performing the answer choice Translation process defined in the Level 1 instructions below. If you are on a later Level, follow the corresponding instructions below.

To Level Up: Complete the full MemAC process defined in your Level instructions without having to peek at the answer choices to accurately remember them on 10 questions in a row.

For example, if you correctly recap all the answer choices on 10 questions in a row without having to peek on Level 1, move to Level 2 on the next question.

Each time you complete one full section of MemAC, complete a MemAC Live Check-In Question(defined below).

Just translate and quip the answers normally. Do not do MemAC.

After choosing your answer, attempt to translate all the answer choices from memory. 

Write down how many answers you're able to translate from memory on each Live Check-In Question.

Compare the number of answers you're able to translate from memory across all your Live Check-In Questions to measure your progress.

Ellen's Advice
If You Want to Win

Don't halfway commit to doing MemAC. The first few hours are by far the most stressful and slow. Do not give up. There is so much benefit on the other side.

Do not read the stimulus or question stem during MemAC.

Do not Party Trick the answer choices during MemAC.

Many students move MemAC to a warmup after they beat Level 5.

They report that they feel like they're at peak mental clarity when they're MemACing.

MemAC is the midpoint of answer choice mastery.

Typically, I'll have my students complete the Answer Choice Primer, then MemAC, then Party Tricking.

After you beat Level 5 of MemAC, consider trying out Party Tricking Jail.

If you're currently missing more than 10 questions per LR or RC questions, brace yourself that MemAC will be difficult and you will have to work hard to improve your skills. Do not let this difficulty dissuade you from investing in the workout.

Beginner students complete 6 MemAC questions per hour 

Intermediate students complete 12 MemAC questions per hour

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: MemAC Circles are an advanced workout. Do not attempt MemAC Circles until you have beaten MemAC Level 5.

  1. MemAC the answer choices at either Level 3 or Level 5, depending on your preference*.

  2. Translate, quip, and CLIR the stimulus.

  3. Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

  4. On each individual answer choice:

    1. Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

    2. Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

      1. If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • MemAC Circles help keep your MemAC skills sharp while allowing you to make the stimulus less intimidating.

    • Once you can MemAC the answer choices, reading the stimulus is much more accessible, almost like you've been given a sneak preview.

  • MemAC Circles slow down the LR process to enhance answer choice understanding and make you less impulsive in your answer choice selection.

  • It can be difficult to ensure that you properly CLIR and Mission on MemAC Circles because the subconscious recognition of the correct answer can be involuntary, even while you're still in the middle of the stimulus.

    • Stay strong in your process. You don't want to get too hasty and miss questions because you didn't give every answer a proper post-stimulus chance.
