inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

You skip parts of the process (like CLIR, Mission, Translation, or quipping) because you feel like you don't really have to do them

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Translate the passage*

  2. RC HIIT Phase 1: Complete the following RC Thunderdome outputs in under 30 seconds each before beginning the questions. These outputs may require looking at the passage.

    1. Outline the structure of the passage overall.

      1. You can use paragraphs as an organizing structure, but you can also delineate on a more fine-grained level, if desired.

    2. Parallel one piece of the passage.

      1. Pick an example, one line of reasoning, or a given person's point of view.

    3. Sub out one word in the passage and replace it with a new word/phrase that means the same thing.

    4. Pick one sentence out of the passage and identify its function.

    5. What is the Main Point?

  3. RC HIIT Phase 2: Complete the following RC Thunderdome outputs in under 30 seconds each. You have two options in how you complete the Phrase 2 outputs: You may complete all the additional RC Thunderdome outputs before beginning the questions or complete two to three additional RC Thunderdome outputs in between each of the questions. These outputs do not require you to look at the passage.

    1. What is the tone of the passage?

    2. Who is the author?

    3. Who is the audience?

    4. Who are the players in the passage and what do they believe?

    5. Strengthen the author's opinion

      1. If the passage feels neutral, write a confirming piece of evidence for the information the author is presenting.

    6. Weaken the author's opinion

      1. If the passage feels neutral, write a disconfirming piece of evidence for the information the author is presenting.

    7. One Inference from the passage

    8. One thing the author is likely to believe

    9. Identify a principle underlying the passage as a whole or an argument within the passage

Sections to use

Ideal for Previously Seen Sections

how to time

Count-Up Stopwatch

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is not important to look at the questions and answer choices during an RC HIIT.

    • The point of this workout is not to answer questions, but if you want to combine it with answer-choosing, I'm not fully against it.

  • Don't attempt to HIIT as a beginner.

    • If you haven't met the Translation time goal or don't have significant experience with full LR sections, wait to HIIT until you need it.

  • For the right kind of plateaued, advanced test taker, HIIT offer a singular opportunity for a perspective shift.

  • HIITs show you where you're weak.

    • If you find that you always struggle with one of the RC HIIT outputs, review the videos and written material on that topic.

  • HIITs are great for when you start to run out of unseen PTs near the end of your prep.

    • HIITs can still be done on previously seen material.

  • If you are an advanced student PTing at 172+, HIITing can really take your skills to the next level.

  • Like Translation + CLIR Drills, HIITs are a great spot to use AI voice dictation to speed up the workout. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

How you know you need to do this

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
What Problem Are We Solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

inline_prep.name: Intuition, Not Impulse
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

inline_prep.name: Stop Oversimplifying
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

Accuracy
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
Prep Map
/
Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Translate the passage*.

  2. Proceed to the first question and translate the question stem.

  3. Make a Mission.

    1. Making a Mission means answering the question yourself.

    2. Go back to the passage to enable yourself to answer the question, if needed. Only look back at the passage in the Mission stage of the question.

    3. Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

  4. On every individual answer choice:

    1. Read, translate and quip the answer choice.

    2. Investigate whether this answer choice meets the standard of what the question stem is asking.

      1. If you think this answer meets the standard of the question stem, highlight the first word of the answer.

      2. If you are not sure whether this answer meets the standard of the question stem, leave it open.

      3. If you know this answer does not meets the standard of the question stem, cross it out.

  5. Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

  6. Hyperskip, if needed.

    1. Aim to hyperskip a total of 5-7 questions per section.

    2. Only go back to your hyperskips at the end of the entire section, not at the end of the passage they're associated with.

    3. You can go back to the passage during the hyperskip.

  7. Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

Instructions

Translate the passage*.

Proceed to the first question and translate the question stem.

Make a Mission.

Making a Mission means answering the question yourself.

Go back to the passage to enable yourself to answer the question, if needed. Only look back at the passage in the Mission stage of the question.

Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

On every individual answer choice:

Read, translate and quip the answer choice.

Investigate whether this answer choice meets the standard of what the question stem is asking.

If you think this answer meets the standard of the question stem, highlight the first word of the answer.

If you are not sure whether this answer meets the standard of the question stem, leave it open.

If you know this answer does not meets the standard of the question stem, cross it out.

Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

Hyperskip, if needed.

Aim to hyperskip a total of 5-7 questions per section.

Only go back to your hyperskips at the end of the entire section, not at the end of the passage they're associated with.

You can go back to the passage during the hyperskip.

Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. For each passage*, write out an answer to each of the following:

    1. What's the Main Point?

    2. What's the tone of the passage?

    3. Who is the author?

    4. Who is the audience?

    5. Who are the players in the passage and what do they believe?

    6. Strengthen the author's opinion

      1. If the passage feels neutral, write a confirming piece of evidence for the information the author is presenting.

    7. Weaken the author's opinion

      1. If the passage feels neutral, write a disconfirming piece of evidence for the information the author is presenting.

    8. Three Inferences from the passage

    9. Three things the author is likely to believe

    10. Parallel one piece of the passage

      1. Pick an example, one line of reasoning, or a given person's point of view.

    11. Outline the structure of the passage

      1. You can use paragraphs as an organizing structure, but you can also delineate on a more fine-grained level, if desired.

    12. Sub out three words in the passage and replace them with a new word/phrase that means the same thing.

    13. Pick three sentences out of the passage and identify their function

    14. Identify a principle underlying the passage as a whole or an argument within the passage

Sections to use

Ideal for Previously Seen Sections

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is not important to look at the questions and answer choices during an RC Thunderdome.

    • The point of this workout is not to answer questions, but if you want to combine it with answer-choosing, I'm not fully against it.

  • Don't attempt to RC Thunderdome as a beginner.

    • If you haven't met the RC Translation time goals or don't have significant experience with full RC sections, wait to RC Thunderdome until you need it.

  • For the right kind of plateaued, advanced test taker, RC Thunderdomes offer a singular opportunity for a perspective shift.

  • RC Thunderdomes show you where you're weak.

    • If you find that you always struggle with one of the RC Thunderdome outputs, review the videos and written material on that topic.

  • RC Thunderdomes are great for when you start to run out of unseen PTs near the end of your prep.

    • RC Thunderdomes can still be done on previously seen material.

  • If you are an advanced student PTing at 172+, RC Thunderdoming can really take your skills to the next level.

  • Like Translation + CLIR Drills, RC Thunderdomes are a great spot to use AI voice dictation to speed up the workout. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

Instructions

  1. On comparative passages*, add the following tasks to your typical RC Thunderdome:

    1. Identify three things the authors disagree about

    2. Identify three things the authors agree about

    3. Identify three concepts mentioned in A but not B

    4. Identify three concepts mentioned in B but not A

    5. Identify titles for each passage

    6. Identify Parallel Reasoning titles for each passage

      1. This means that you'll Parallel your titles from the last questions into a new situation the same way you would parallel a Logical Reasoning stimulus in the answer choices.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is not important to look at the questions and answer choices during an RC Thunderdome.

    • The point of this workout is not to answer questions, but if you want to combine it with answer-choosing, I'm not fully against it.

  • Don't attempt to RC Thunderdome as a beginner.

    • If you haven't met the RC Translation time goals or don't have significant experience with full RC sections, wait to RC Thunderdome until you need it.

  • For the right kind of plateaued, advanced test taker, RC Thunderdomes offer a singular opportunity for a perspective shift.

  • RC Thunderdomes show you where you're weak.

    • If you find that you always struggle with one of the RC Thunderdome outputs, review the videos and written material on that topic.

  • RC Thunderdomes are great for when you start to run out of unseen PTs near the end of your prep.

    • RC Thunderdomes can still be done on previously seen material.

  • If you are an advanced student PTing at 172+, RC Thunderdoming can really take your skills to the next level.

  • Like Translation + CLIR Drills, RC Thunderdomes are a great spot to use AI voice dictation to speed up the workout. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • The Reverse Shuffle's bark is a lot worse than its bite. Don't be so intimidated by this workout that you don't even try it. 

  • The Reverse Shuffle is a great way to prove to yourself that you don't actually have to look back to the passage as much as you think you do.

    • For the most part, you look back at the passage to ease anxiety, not because it actually increases the number of correct answers per section. 

  • The Reverse Shuffle combines the best of Party Tricking with the best of Translation.

    • You know your Translation has to be really good because of the gap between translating the passage and actually answering its questions, so it automatically holds you to a higher standard. 

    • The steps between translating the passage and actually answering its questions produce a beneficial blur over the content of the passage.

    • This beneficial blur mimics the feeling of Party Tricking – it forces you to answer the questions conceptually, rather than relying on keywording to choose your answer.

    • This is why the Reverse Shuffle often yields an increase in accuracy. 

  • Just like the E Blackout, I'm sure you won't believe that the Reverse Shuffle was actually used on a real LSAT to produce a 180. But it did, and I have the receipts ✅.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
What Problem Are We Solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

Strengthen Your Working Memory
What Problem Are We Solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

You ping-pong between your final two answers, constantly rereading them because they disappear from your memory immediately
You think your problem is "just the answer choices"
You rely heavily on looking back at the stimulus/passage in the answer choices
You re-read the same sentence multiple times hoping it will stick

inline_prep.name: Learn From Your Mistakes
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

FIX 3 OF 7
Learn From Your Mistakes
What Problem Are We Solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

How You Know You Need To Do This

You attack yourself with negative self-talk any time you look at your wrong answers

sections.html:
Instructions

For each passage*:

  1. Read and translate the first sentence of the passage.

  2. Read and translate the last sentence of the passage.

  3. Think for a second about the passage.

  4. Translate the entire passage.

    1. Use whichever style of RC Translation you're currently using.

  5. Answer the questions according to your typical RC question process.

Spoiled Comparative Reads

  1. Read and translate the first and last sentences of Passage A.

  2. Read and translate the first and last sentences of Passage B.

  3. Think for a second about the relationships between the passages.

  4. Translate both passages.

    1. Use whichever style of RC Translation you're currently using.

  5. Answer the questions according to your typical RC question process.

New Sections Only

inline_prep.name: Strengthen Your Working Memory
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Strengthen Your Working Memory
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

inline_prep.name: Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine
inline_prep.html:
Speed
Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Speed

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines are the best way to push yourself to improve stamina and test-day readiness at the same time.

The first few sections of a Test-Day Timing Marathon may be rocky, but you should gradually acclimate to how a test-day timed section feels.

Don't attempt Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines if your Marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing. Test-Day Timing Marathons are more appropriate when you're within 5 minutes of test-day timing.

Test-Day Timing Marathons don't allow for natural time progression in the same way Marathon Routines do, so they risk compromising your accuracy and process far more than the other Speed Routines.

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

How to Pull This Off

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. Complete six to eight test-day timed LR sections* in one sitting with no breaks, or complete six to eight test-day timed RC sections in one sitting with no breaks.

    1. This means you should use test-day timing on all sections, not Marathon timing.

    2. Immediately proceed to the next section in the Marathon as soon as the test-day timer expires.

    3. Any questions left unanswered within time will be marked wrong.

NOTE: You can modify the Test-Day Timing Marathon to alternate between LR and RC sections, as you would in a Mixed Section Marathon. Just flip a coin (or ask your favorite digital assistant to flip a coin) to decide each section when you're ready to begin that section mid-Marathon.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • It is very important that you do not take breaks between sections or check your sections in the middle of the Marathon.

    • Marathons only work because your brain doesn’t get the chance to re-adapt to non-LSAT thinking.

    • Taking breaks guarantees that the Marathon will not work.

      • Do not check your phone.

      • Do not have conversations.

      • Do not take a lunch break.

    • Put snacks and drinks on the desk to eat while you Marathon, if needed.

    • The only breaks allowed during Marathons are medically required or biologically required breaks.

      • Running to the bathroom is allowed between sections.

      • Accommodated breaks for medically required tasks (like insulin injections, etc) are obviously allowed.

  • Open all the sections you plan to complete in separate tabs before starting the Marathon.

  • It is exceptionally important that you do not see the score of each section in the middle of the Marathon.

    • If you see the scores, it will take out of the focused activity and all the intuition-building work will be undone. The Marathon will be wasted.

  • Keep track of the order of the sections in your Marathon, so you can analyze the results.

  • If you feel yourself getting worse as the Marathon progresses, you are likely becoming fatigued.

    • This is ok, but it indicates that you’ll need to do another Marathon. Fatigue is part of the process; it indicates that you need to build stamina.

  • At the end of the Marathon, take a break and then Camo all the sections in a big batch.

Timing Tips

  • Set a section timer for test-day timing in LawHub's Self-Paced Mode.

    • Do not use LawHub's Exam Mode.

inline_prep.html:
Speed
Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Speed

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines are the best way to push yourself to improve stamina and test-day readiness at the same time.

The first few sections of a Test-Day Timing Marathon may be rocky, but you should gradually acclimate to how a test-day timed section feels.

Don't attempt Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines if your Marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing. Test-Day Timing Marathons are more appropriate when you're within 5 minutes of test-day timing.

Test-Day Timing Marathons don't allow for natural time progression in the same way Marathon Routines do, so they risk compromising your accuracy and process far more than the other Speed Routines.

How to Pull This Off

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

5
Camo Review

How To Pull This Off

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How To Move On

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

inline_prep.name: Learn From Your Mistakes
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

FIX 3 OF 7
Learn From Your Mistakes
What Problem Are We Solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

Instructions

NOTE: Do not attempt The Ultimate Stress Test if you have not beaten MemAC or if you have never done a Write In.

  1. Write In the odd questions in the section*.

  2. MemAC the even questions in the section.

  3. Return to the Write-In questions:

    1. MemAC the answer choices.

    2. Choose an answer using only your Write In without looking back at the stimulus.

  4. Return to the even MemAC questions:

    1. Attempt to Write In the correct answer from what you remember of the MemAC.

Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • The Ultimate Stress Test is not for the faint of heart and is an entirely optional workout.

    • Very few people at Elemental do the Ultimate Stress Test, but it can be helpful to a small minority of students who want to push themselves before their exam.

  • Do all the questions in order.

    • This means you'll be alternating between MemAC and Write Ins throughout the section.

  • In order to do the Ultimate Stress Test, you must be familiar with the Write In and MemAC instructions.

    • Reference the Write In and MemAC workout instructions, if needed, before completing this workout.

For each stimulus in the section*, write or speak out each and every one of the following outputs, according to the stimulus type, without looking at the question stem or answer choices:

    • Weaken correct answer

    • Strengthen correct answer

    • Necessary assumption

    • Sufficient assumption

    • Method correct answer

    • Argument parts identifications

    • Parallel Skeleton

    • Parallel correct answer

      • Use your favorite topic as a consistent analogous base

      • This means all your Parallel correct answers can be about dogs or cars across all the questions in the section.

  • On a Debate, write or speak your own:

    • Controversy

    • Agreement

    • Loophole in both speakers

  • On a Paradox, write or speak your own:

    • Resolution

    • Inference

    • Contradiction

  • On a Premise Set, write or speak your own:

    • Three Inferences

    • Contradiction

inline_prep.name: Stop Oversimplifying
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

Thunderdome Answer Key
PT7.S1
Q1
1. Weaken: In the first years after the invention of the printing press, people who knew how to read but couldn’t afford expensive manuscript copies began stocking up on printed books
2. Strengthen: The affordability of printed books encouraged people who were previously unable read to learn to do so
3. NA: Increased demand for printed books wasn’t the result of a single rich family hoarding copies for their personal libraries
4. SA: A dramatic increase in demand for reading materials always results from increased literacy in a population
5. Method: Assumes the correlation between two phenomena means that one of those phenomena was the result of another
6. Argument Part: The public’s demand for printed books in the first years after the invention of the printing press was many times greater than demand had been for manuscript copies. – premise that the author claims as evidence for a certain phenomenon
7. Parallel Skeleton: Before X, few purchased the expensive versions of Y. Now, Y are cheaper, and more people buy them. Therefore, more people learned how to use Y.
8. Parallel Correct Answer: Before Fluffy went to Esther the dog trainer, he rarely sat on command. Esther has a reputation for inducing obedience in even the most defiant canines. Now, Fluffy is a model pup who sits whenever he’s told. This change in Fluffy’s behavior demonstrates that he must have had wax in his ears which prevented him from hearing commands, and Esther cured it.


Q2
1. Weaken: Bevex-sweetened soft drinks are now sold in liters which contain the equivalent of six cans of the substance, and die-hard consumers usually guzzle at least five liters a day
2. Strengthen: Humans process Bevex with a unique enzyme that inhibits its carcinogenic effects, which mice lack
3. NA: People drink fewer than 25 cans of Bevex-sweetened soda a day
4. SA: No consumer of Bevex-sweetened soda drinks more than five cans a day, and all artificial sweeteners have the same effect on humans as they do on mice
5. Method: Takes for granted that nobody drinks more than a certain amount of something a day. Assumes two different species process a substance in the same way
6. Argument Part: Bevex is in fact safe for people – conclusion the argument is designed to support
7. Parallel Skeleton: X is only bad for Y in large amounts. Z would have to drink a large quantity of X-containing substance to experience the same toxic effects. Thus, X is safe for Z to consume
8. Parallel Correct Answer: Hershey’s chocolate contains a chemical compound that is poisonous to dogs, but only if it is consumed in excess. A recent study demonstrated that Dachshunds can consume up to 10 grams of the chemical before its toxic effects kick in. Great Danes would have to consume five king-size Hershey’s bars to ingest an equivalent amount. Thus, we can say confidently that Great Danes are safe to indulge in Hershey’s chocolate
Q3
1. Controversy: Whether absolutely anyone can travel around the world
2. Agreement: Airlines make it possible to travel to different places
3. Loophole for Harry: What if most people can’t afford to pay for expensive airline tickets?
4. Loophole for Judith: What if the flights that everyone can afford enable globe-trotting?
Q4
1. Weaken: The new pills contain less than a quarter of the fiber that nutritionists recommend people consume daily
2. Strengthen: The same group of nutritionists claim that supplementing one’s diet with any quantity of additional fiber will yield health benefits
3. NA: The nutritionists’ recommendation does not apply exclusively to naturally occurring fiber in foods like lentils and chia seeds
4. SA: If a dietary supplement contains at least some fiber, it’s guaranteed to satisfy the nutritionists’ recommendation
5. Method: Presupposes that a supplement containing any amount of fiber will meet the nutritionists’ recommendation
6. Argument Part: Nutritionists have recommended that people eat more fiber – premise on which the advertising campaign hinges on
7. Parallel Skeleton: Experts say consuming more X is good for you. You should buy Y because it contains some amount of X
8. Parallel Correct Answer: 9/10 veterinarians say that feeding your dog fish oil will increase the shine and thickness of its coat. The nutrition label on Kelpy Kibble indicates that it contains 2 milligrams of fish oil
Q5
1. Inference 1: One cannot have a moral duty that is usually impossible to fulfill
2. Inference 2: Moral duties apply only to actions that individuals can consciously control
3. Inference 3: For a moral duty to exist, there must be a reliable way for individuals to determine how to act in accordance with it
4. Contradiction: Consumers have a moral obligation to comply with all recommendations made by environmentalists, regardless of whether they are practically feasible
Q6
1. Weaken: People want to boost the performance of their heart and lungs to achieve their fitness goals, and enhanced brain function isn’t correlated with such outcomes
2. Strengthen: A group of neurologists recently published a study affirming the efficacy of magazines like Stimulus in improving brain performance
3. NA: Brain performance can improve through methods that improve performance in other physical organs
4. SA: Everybody wants to improve brain performance, and subscribing to any magazine that claims to exercise your brain is guaranteed to achieve that goal
5. Method: Takes for granted that everyone wants to accomplish a certain goal. Implies that two physical organs are similar in one respect because they are similar in another. Claims that one technique for achieving an outcome is effective without offering evidence
6. Argument Part: Anyone who exercises knows from firsthand experience that exercise leads to better performance of such physical organs as the heart and the lungs, as well as to improvement in muscle tone. – cites an analogy intended to demonstrate the veracity of a claim
7. Parallel Skeleton: X and Y share a defining characteristic. Because you can improve the performance of X through Z, Z will have the same effect on Y. Buy this product, it does Z!
8. Parallel Correct Answer: It is widely accepted that giving your cat a scratching post will alleviate stress and stress-related behavioral issues. Just like cats, dogs are domesticated mammals that can experience stress. Order a Scratchinator today: the post that keeps your pooch pacified!
Q7
1. Weaken: Major reforms to the health-care system enacted in the 1990s increased the incentive for providers and insurers to assume the costs of care
2. Strengthen: The state of the health-care system hasn’t changed significantly since the 1980s
3. NA: Health-care providers and insurers still have an incentive to transfer the cost burden of care to other parties
4. SA: Health-care providers and insurers always capitalize on any opportunity to increase profits, and passing off costs is still an opportunity in the current health-care system
5. Method: Uses an analogy to demonstrate the challenges of addressing a societal issue
6. Argument Part: The reason is that this system gives health-care providers and insurers every incentive to shift, wherever possible, the costs of treating illness onto each other or any other party, including the patient – premise the author substantiates by way of example in the last sentence
7. Parallel Skeleton: There’s no feasible solution to the problem of X within systemic constraints. Y, a critical stakeholder in X, has no practical reason to decrease X, as demonstrated by this action taken 30 years ago.
8. Parallel Correct Answer: There’s no effective way to address the issue of inbreeding in the doodle population. That’s because doodle breeders get a reputational boost by producing puppies that are both trainable and aesthetically pleasing, and that happens when their parents are related. Just consider Pierre, the last championship Labradoodle, whose parents were first cousins!
