Instructions

  1. Translate and quip the passage or stimulus*.

    1. If you encounter a word you are unsure of, highlight it.

  2. Finish the passage or stimulus.

    1. Be sure to highlight ALL the words you're unsure of.

    2. If you wouldn't bet money on the definition of the word, that means you are unsure of the definition of that word.

  3. Add the highlighted words to your Vocab Tracker and write in the definitions according to the instructions outlined in the How to Learn Vocab Without AI video.

  4. Restart the Vocabulary Translation Drill on the same stimulus or passage now that you know what the words mean.

  5. Continue this pattern for the entire section.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Vocabulary Translation Drills are designed to fill in gaps in vocabulary that impede understanding the stimulus.

  • It feels significantly different to engage with a stimulus when you know what all the words in the stimulus mean. Vocabulary Translation Drills allow students to experience that reality.

  • It is worth building your vocabulary skills. You can learn enough words to improve your score.

    • Yes, you don't know that the words you learn will be on your exam.

    • No one ever has any guarantee of what words will be on their exam, and it's on us to improve ourselves despite this fact.

    • Vocabulary building is cumulative and you will increase the chance that you know all the words that appear on your exam by gradually enhancing your vocabulary, no matter where you are starting out.

  • Vocabulary Translation Drill are a great idea for non-native English speakers, especially students who do not live in an English-speaking environment.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

sections.html:
Instructions

NOTE: The Write In replaces the Mission step of the Full LR Process.

  1. Read and translate the stimulus in chunks*. 

  2. Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

  3. Continue until the end of the stimulus.

  4. Mark the conclusion.

  5. Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

  6. Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

  7. Write in a correct answer to the question.

    1. Make the Write In answer sound like a real answer choice, not a messy note.

  8. On every individual answer choice:

    1. Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

    2. Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

      1. If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

      2. If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

      3. If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

  9. Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

  10. Hyperskip, if needed.

    1. Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

  11. Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Write Ins are great workouts for forcing you to process the question stem's ask on a deeper level.

  • The point is to force you to actually answer the question yourself, proving that you know the answer to the question without any suggestion.

    • The point of a Write In is not to match your Write In answer to the answer choices.

    • You don't really have any business vetting someone else's answers to a question if you can't answer the question on your own, right?

    • Write Ins force you to hone this vital skill.

  • If you can design a correct answer yourself, it proves you really know what the question is asking, what the stimulus/passage entails, and how answer choices move. All of these are necessary conditions of LSAT mastery.

  • Writing down one word in reaction to the question stem is not a Write In.

  • If you struggle with answer choice language, writing your own correct answer during the Write In is a great opportunity to improve.

inline_prep.name: Stop Oversimplifying
inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

sections.html:
Instructions

  1. After you've Camoed your LR or RC section, begin the Wrong Answer Journaling process.

  2. For each wrong answer, fill in the date you did the section, the question number that was wrong, and the answer you chose.

    1. This information will already be filled in for you if you Camo using Loophole Online.

  3. Fill in your Reason Missed column

    1. In this column, write down what you did wrong that caused you to miss this question.

      1. Ask yourself, "Why did I think that this wrong answer was right? Why did I think that this right answer was wrong?" Focus on changing the actions that enabled these mistaken judgments.

    2. The first word of every entry in this column should be "I." 

      1. Example: "I misidentified the question stem."

      2. This will force you to reflect on what you did that caused you to choose the wrong answer and overlook the right answer.

  4. Fill in your Solution column

    1. In this column, write down what you will do differently to ensure you don't make this same mistake again.

      1. Ask yourself, "What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the wrong answer is wrong? What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the right answer is right?"

    2. The first words of every entry in this column should be "I will..." 

      1. Example: "I will do Question Stem Training to improve my ability to correctly identify question types."

    3. Frame your Solution Column as a direct response to the Reason Missed column.

sections.html:
Ellen's Advice

If You Want to Win

  • Keep your Wrong Answer Journal entries short and sweet. One to two sentences is enough for each column.

  • Do not waste time in your Wrong Answer Journal writing down detailed explanations of why the answer you chose was wrong, and why the right answer is right in the exact context of the question.

    • If you're writing anything that cannot be ported directly to subsequent sections, you are wasting your Wrong Answer Journal time. 

  • The Wrong Answer Journal gives you a chance to identify the exact actions you took that made you make the wrong decision. It then gives you the opportunity to decide which actions you will take in the future that will enable you to make correct decisions. This is the essence of improvement on the LSAT.

    • I want you to know why an answer is right and another is wrong, but I don't want you to stop there. I want you to start there.

    • After you know why the correct answer is correct and why the wrong answer is wrong, look more deeply at your actions and mindset in relation to the question.

    • What did you do that caused this result? And what will you do to ensure a different result next time?

  • Do not rely on cheap explanations in your Reason Missed column like "silly mistake," "misread," or "rushing."

    • Dive into why you made this silly mistake, why you misread, and why you were rushing.

    • This is how you can identify the problematic actions that lead to problematic judgments and change them for the better.

Do not rely on cheap explanations in your Reason Missed column like "silly mistake," "misread," or "rushing."

Dive into why you made this silly mistake, why you misread, and why you were rushing.

This is how you can identify the problematic actions that lead to problematic judgments and change them for the better.

prep_map_points.html:
Accuracy
Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits

What problem are we solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Disrupt Your Toxic Habits
What Problem Are We Solving?

It's so easy to attribute a score you don't like to anything but your toxic habits. To say, "This one was just hard" or "I always have trouble with that question type." But none of those factors chose the wrong answer. You chose the wrong answer. And if you want your score to change, you have to change the toxic habits that made you choose that answer.

Toxic habits are like lifting weights with bad form – they feel like they're making lifting easier. But It's only a matter of time until you get injured. If you have bad form, you can't up your weight safely. Instead, you have to lower the weight and fix your form. (I would know... I had to have surgery to fix two hernias from bad weight-lighting form.)

The sad thing is that many toxic habits are recommended to well-meaning students who simply don't know any better. Just like the trainer who told me it was totally fine to up my weight way too fast.

If an "expert" tells you that you that only have to read the first word of most RC answers, who are you to know that's toxic? 

You just started LSAT prep. You don't know any better. And you accidentally adopt a toxic habit that lowers your score.

That is the information asymmetry that keeps me grinding beyond the point of rationality. I hate that information asymmetry because it lets people take advantage of you.

Advice like that decreases your score and you have to feel the pain of score variation to figure out that it was toxic in the first place.

That's why I've created and tested a non-toxic, proven LSAT process for the past 30,000+ hours. The processes in Loophole Online are built to replace toxic habits from the ground up.

Implementing non-toxic habits will get you the answer 100 out of 100 times when you implement it as instructed. That's what this Accuracy Fix trains you to do.

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage

What problem are we solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

  • you're falling asleep in the middle?

Accuracy
Learn From Your Mistakes
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Learn From Your Mistakes

What problem are we solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

Learn From Your Mistakes
What Problem Are We Solving?

Seeing the score is like popping a balloon. 

You want to see the score so bad. Because you need to "see how you're doing," "understand where you are," "stay motivated," and "know what to work on."

So, of course, you need to check the score as soon as you're done with the section.  But suddenly, as soon as you see that number.

There's nothing interesting left anymore. 

Now you "know where you are," but the emotional reaction to where you are overwhelms any hope of strategic insights. 

If you like the number, you'll walk away excited and think, "Okay, now I'm good."

And then the next section is likely to crash and burn from laziness and complacency. You don't need to work that hard when you're good, right? 

If you don't like the number, tears follow.

Now there's no motivation to continue because nothing ever works. So what's the point? Why try? I should just give up and save the effort I would waste on this. I never get better. 

When you do this, you actively decline to change the behaviors that caused your wrong answers. This causes you to not improve.

Failing to look inward to understand what you need to change will cause you to leave points on the table.

This Accuracy Fix stops that rollercoaster of pain and plateaus.

You can get better. Give yourself the chance to really understand what you're doing wrong.

Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

What problem are we solving?

You should not take an official LSAT until you have practiced regularly in test conditions. This means you're practicing in a quiet environment, taking exactly the allocated time you'll have on test day (no more no less), and you are not taking breaks to go on your phone or talk to people. Practicing in chaotic, unplanned conditions causes more score chaos than you'd think.

Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

Failsafe Marathon Routines combine the best of Failsafes with the best of Marathons.

These Routines can be brutal, especially if you don't beat the Failsafe frequently. But the same thing that makes them punishing also makes them effective.

They're a blunt instrument that will change you as a test taker, so they are often relied upon in emergency situations.

When a test date is within one week and you still aren't able to complete the section in time with goal-level accuracy, this is your Routine.

How to Pull This Off

Failsafe Marathons Routines work well to speed up the progress of a Failsafe Routine.

Sometimes, students will see a lot of traction with Failsafes, but the pace of bringing the time down little by little each day can feel limiting, especially with a near-term test date.

Failsafe Marathon Routines are like the "In Case of Emergency Break the Glass" of the Prep Map.

They are harsh, but they will push you harder than almost any other workout.

How to move on

If you have lost every Failsafe you've attempted in your Failsafe Marathon for three consecutive prep days, here are a few options for what you can try next:

  1. Set a higher baseline natural pace to start your Failsafe Marathon

  2. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with a Light Failsafe

  3. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with Pacing Practice

  4. Return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

If you sometimes hit goal time and accuracy in your Failsafe Marathon, progress to any of the following Speed Routines: Marathon Routine, Mixed Timing Marathon Routine, or Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine. 

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Failsafe Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

But you can channel your desire to get the question right into building an invulnerable fortress of analysis throughout every stage of the question. This fortress (Translation, CLIR, Mission, Back Up Plan) will allow you to see exactly why these answers are wrong without. any. drama.

The answer choices only gain manipulative power over you when you look to them to save you. But you are not the freaking damsel that answer C is here to rescue. You're the hero.

You're here to judge answer C, and you're going to judge it according to your vetted, bulletproof standards.

The answers need to impress you, not the other way around.

This Accuracy Fix trains you to build the fortress.

Because you are smart enough. You have the tools, the time, and the resources to never need any answer choice to save you again.

Timing Failsafe Routine

Why are we doing this?

Timing Failsafe Routines are one of the only ways to effectively reduce time without Marathoning.

The upsides of Timing Failsafes are:

  • They can be done in shorter periods of time than a Marathon

  • They allow for more systematic gradual time reduction

  • Review can be more targeted and frequent

This Routine works great for students who thrive on structure.

How to Pull This Off

Failsafe Routines work best when combined with other Routines to bring time down while maintaining accuracy.

Essentially, you have to address the reasons why the Failsafe breaks in order to get it to progress, so you'll want to consider alternating Failsafe Routines with the Accuracy Fix Routines that pertain to your mistakes.

How to move on

Timing Failsafe Routines can get you to test-day goal time and accuracy without progressing to any other Speed Routine.

However, if you have lost every Timing Failsafe you've attempted for three consecutive prep days, here are a few options for what you can try next:

  1. Set a higher baseline natural pace to start your Timing Failsafe

  2. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with a Light Failsafe

  3. Replace the Timing Failsafe in this Routine with Pacing Practice

  4. Return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

If you sometimes hit goal time and accuracy in your Timing Failsafes, progress to any of the following Speed Routines: Failsafe Marathon Routine, Mini-Marathon Routine, or Marathon Routine.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Timing Failsafe Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Marathon Routine
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Speed

Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

The Marathon Routine is the most effective Routine in the Prep Map for pure speed improvement.

No other Routine or workout will increase speed like this Routine.

The purpose of the Marathon Routine is to decrease the time it takes to get questions right by exhausting you to the point where your subconscious intuition will have to kick in to complete the questions.

This Routine will eventually enable you to finish the section in time at goal accuracy.

LR
RC
FrequencySpaced Set
Challenge IndexEllen Whyyy
LevelAdvanced
Study block4-5+ hours
Time goal to move on20 min

Routine Schedule

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

1

The Island

10 minutes
2

Translation + CLIR Drill

1 section
3

Marathon

8 sections
4

Camo Review

5

Wrong Answer Journal

How to Pull This Off

Marathons have a ton of specific, crucial instructions, so make sure you internalize the Marathon timing procedures, section data to track, and advice on how to win contained in the Marathon Workout instructions.

When adding Marathon Routines to your prep, be strategic about section usage.

Since one Marathon uses several PTs, you have to stay mindful about your consumption of these non-renewable resources. It can be advisable to mix previously-seen material into some Marathons to minimize material usage.

Make sure you don't Marathon all the most recent PTs; this will leave you with no fresh exams to use as full test-conditions practice tests.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

Marathon Routines can get you to test-day goal time and accuracy without progressing to any other Speed Routine.

However, you should change your Speed Routine, if you notice any of the following issues in your Marathon Routine:

  1. Your speed and accuracy on new sections have plateaued or gotten worse for three Marathons in a row

    1. Try a Timing Failsafe Routine or return to the Accuracy Fix Routines

  2. You don't have uninterrupted blocks of time on your calendar for Marathons and you are unwilling to adjust your calendar

    1. Move to a Timing Failsafe Routine

  3. Your score decreases when you switch from LR to RC or RC to LR

    1. Move to a Mixed Section Marathon Routine

If you're still not hitting your time and accuracy goals, or you're just starting to reach your time goals while maintaining accuracy on a few sections, you probably need to do more Marathon Routines.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

Once Mini-Marathons are no longer exhausting, or they are only exhausting on the last section, it's time to move on to a full Marathon Routine.

If you're still not hitting both your time and accuracy goals, or you're only just starting to reach those goals on one or two sections in the Mini-Marathon, progress to a full Marathon Routine.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Mini-Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Mixed Section Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

Mixed Section Marathon Routines are fantastic for students who struggle with context switching and stamina.

If you have any worry about being depleted during the last section on test day, Mixed Section Marathons are better than PTs and standard Marathons for stamina training.

After you've done 1.5x to 2x the sections of a PT in a single sitting with no breaks, it will feel like nothing to do four sections on test day with a break between sections 1 and 2.

How to Pull This Off

Mixed Section Marathons should be approached similarly to regular Marathons, so be sure to familiarize yourself with the Marathon timing procedures, section data to track, and advice on how to win contained in the Marathon Workout instructions.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

Mixed Section Marathons are not the most effective Routines for reducing time.

If you are still having trouble meeting you test-day timing goal, you should progress to another Speed Routine that is more suited to pure time reduction (like the Marathon Routine or the Failsafe Marathon Routine).

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

You can move to any of the other Speed Routines, if your Mixed Section Marathon Routine went well. You do not have to go in order.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

The purpose of Mixed Timing Marathon Routines is to gradually integrate test-day timing standards into your skillset while minimally disrupting accuracy.

By allowing alternation between Marathon timing and test-day timing, you have the opportunity to reaffirm your standards without compromise during the Marathon-timed sections and then get used to pushing those standards into the test-day timing window.

Don't attempt Mixed Timing Marathon Routines if your marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing.

Mixed Timing Marathons are not typically as effective as regular Marathons at large time reduction (10+ minutes) since the alternation makes it more difficult to reach the flow state required for subconscious skill integration (which is what allows the time to drop).

However, Mixed Timing Marathons are great to ease into how test day will feel.

How to Pull This Off

To make the most of a Mixed Timing Marathon Routine, the variation between Marathon-timed sections and test-day timed sections shouldn't be too great.

You don't want the two kinds of timed sections to feel like a yo-yo (one section with very high timing, followed by another section with very low timing).

Ideally, there isn't much of a difference between the Marathon-timed sections and the test-day timed sections. Since you are never allowed to end sections before your countdown test-day timer expires (35 minutes, 53 minutes, etc), the only time variation you should see between sections is higher times on some of the Marathon-timed sections.

Try to keep Marathon timed-sections to a maximum of 10 minutes over your test-day timed sections.

This advice shouldn't be a reason to continuously check the time during Marathon-timed sections – instead, think of this advice as a caution against jumping into this Speed Routine before you're ready.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

If your test-day timed sections crash and burn on the Mixed Timing Marathons, but you have hit goal time and accuracy on the Marathon-timed sections before, don't give up hope.

You may just be anxious about the countdown timer on test-day timed sections and need experience to acclimate.

Try progressing to Marathon Routines to ground yourself in your accurate, controlled process that consistently fits within test-day timed constraints without the countdown timer.

If you sometimes hit goal time and accuracy in your Mixed Timing Marathon, progress to a Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in the majority of your sections, take a Practice Test (PT).

  1. Prep Map/

Strengthen Your Working Memory

What problem are we solving?

You know that feeling when your memory just goes blank in the middle of a question? And you kinda have no idea what you're supposed to do?

Yeah, that's not supposed to happen.

That's something to train out of you.

And this whole LSAT thing is going to feel so much better when you have the evidence you need to make the correct decisions in the moment. 

I never knew memory was such privilege and advantage. 

I used to think, "Of course everyone is subconsciously and instantaneously interrelating every answer choice with the compete conceptual idea behind the stimulus. That's the only way anyone would ever make a decision about an answer choice, right?"

WRONG.

This is the blindspot you have when you "just know" the answer to questions.

Choosing answers the way I just described feels so good that you can't imagine anyone would ever want to do it a different way.

But if you don't remember the complete conceptual idea behind the stimulus/passage while you're in the answer choices, you don't have the option of choosing answers this way.

That's the problem what we're here to solve.

This Accuracy Fix will train your memory to be able to enact this (much more fun and accurate) process in the answer choices.

Yes, the training is strenuous, but all good training is. And on the other side, you won't be able to believe you really chose answers without keeping the whole Translation in your working memory.

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines are the best way to push yourself to improve stamina and test-day readiness at the same time.

The first few sections of a Test-Day Timing Marathon may be rocky, but you should gradually acclimate to how a test-day timed section feels.

Don't attempt Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines if your Marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing. Test-Day Timing Marathons are more appropriate when you're within 5 minutes of test-day timing.

Test-Day Timing Marathons don't allow for natural time progression in the same way Marathon Routines do, so they risk compromising your accuracy and process far more than the other Speed Routines.

RC

Routine Schedule

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

1

The Island

How to Pull This Off

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine
Why Are We Doing This?

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines are the best way to push yourself to improve stamina and test-day readiness at the same time.

The first few sections of a Test-Day Timing Marathon may be rocky, but you should gradually acclimate to how a test-day timed section feels.

Don't attempt Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines if your Marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing. Test-Day Timing Marathons are more appropriate when you're within 5 minutes of test-day timing.

Test-Day Timing Marathons don't allow for natural time progression in the same way Marathon Routines do, so they risk compromising your accuracy and process far more than the other Speed Routines.

How To Pull This Off

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How To Move On

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

Translation + Decaf Routine

Why are we doing this?

Decaf is one of the most intense, difficult Workouts on the whole Prep Map. It's also magical.

By the end of Decaf, you can actually say the whole Translation of the passage out loud from memory. Doesn't that sound like a goal worth sweating for?

How to Pull This Off

Adding Decaf RC Translation to your Routine means you'll have less time for your Translation + CLIR Drills. This should be fine because your Translation + CLIR Drills are taking less time than they used to, so you should ideally be able to maintain the same Translation + CLIR Drill volume as you did in the Intro Translation Routine (Translation Routine 1).

Make sure to watch the Decaf video explanation and demo before trying Decaf on your own (all linked below). It really helps to see me do it before you try it yourself.

Your progression toward the Decaf RC Translation time and accuracy goals is primarily determined by two things: volume and following the instructions. Do at least 1 full section of Decaf RC Translation per day, if possible. Ideally, you would complete 3 consecutive sections of Decaf RC Translation per day.

If you don't practice Decaf every day or don't follow the Decaf instructions, it will stay difficult longer. To maximize your progress in this Routine, only do Decaf Translation Drills on whole sections at a time. Do not split up Decaf Translation Drills into individual passages or take breaks between passages. The number one way to improve quickly at Decaf RC Translation is volume, and if you only do one passage per day the volume will be too low to allow for progress.

Do not compromise the Translation and recap standard outlined in the Decaf RC Translation instructions. If you do not recap with all the details or do not quip, you are not completing Decaf RC Translation and should not progress to the next Routine.

How to move on

Once you hit the Translation + CLIR time goal, ideally while maintaining accuracy of -5 or better against the CLIR Answer Key, you can move on to the AC Primer + Decaf Routine.

We move to the Answer Choice Primer next so we can bring your newfound Translation skills into the answer choices.

Translation + CLIR Goals

  • The time goal for Translation + CLIR Drills is 20 minutes.

  • The accommodated time goals for Translation + CLIR Drills are 25 minutes for 53-minute accommodations and 30 minutes for 70-minute accommodations.

  • Meeting this Translation + CLIR Drill time goal is only valid under two conditions:

    • You have a CLIR for every stimulus.

    • You have translated and quipped every stimulus in the section out loud.

Translation
Foundation Translation Routine
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Translation

Foundation Translation Routine

Why are we doing this?

The Translation + CLIR Drills in this Routine are the foundation of your entire LSAT prep journey. This is the most important homework you will do during your LSAT prep training, even compared to PTs.

This Routine builds a foundation in LR Translation before we port your Translation skills over to RC in the next Routine.

LR
RC
FrequencyDaily Foundation
Challenge IndexPretty Chill
LevelBeginner
Study block2-4 hours
Time goal to move on20 min

Routine Schedule

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

1

Translation + CLIR Drill

≥ 3 sections
2

Extracurricular Reading

3

Vocab Training

Once A Week, Do This Instead

1

Translation Marathon

8 sections
≥ 1x per week

How to Pull This Off

Your progression toward the Translation time and accuracy goals is primarily determined by two things: volume and following the instructions.

To maximize your progress in this Routine, do all your Translation + CLIR Drills consecutively; do not take breaks between Translation + CLIR Drills. Do not review your Translation + CLIR Drills in between sections. All review should be done in a separate sitting.

Do at least 3 consecutive Translation + CLIR Drills per day, if possible. Ideally, you would complete 6 Translation + CLIR drills consecutively per day. Doing 1 Translation + CLIR Drill per day will not improve your skills; it will keep your skills the same. You will only start improving on your second consecutive Translation + CLIR Drill; this is why it is so useful to do at least 3 consecutive Translation + CLIR Drills every day.

Add a Translation Marathon to your Daily Practice at least once per week. If you can manage to do Translation + CLIR Marathons more often, you will progress to the time goal faster.

Extracurricular Reading and Vocab should always be done at the end of your Routine to gradually expand your common sense in the subject areas where you're weakest. If you struggle with science passages, emphasize daily science engagement in the Extracurricular Reading. If you struggle with abstract language, emphasize daily humanities engagement in the Extracurricular Reading.

How to move on

Once you are halfway to your Translation + CLIR Drill time goal, move to the next Routine: Translation + Decaf.

The time goal for Translation + CLIR Drills is 20 minutes. The accommodated time goals for Translation + CLIR Drills are 25 minutes for 53-minute accommodations and 30 minutes for 70-minute accommodations. Meeting this Translation + CLIR Drill time goal is only valid under two conditions: you have a CLIR for every stimulus and you have translated and quipped every stimulus in the section out loud. Ideally, you should hit -5 accuracy against the CLIR Answer Key consistently in order to beat the time goal, but this accuracy goal may be adjusted according to your score goals.

Example of When to Move On: You started at 52 minutes per out loud Translation + CLIR Drill section and you don't have accommodations, so your time goal is 20 minutes. The midpoint of 52 and 20 is 36, so you would move on when your time hits 36 minutes.

ROUTINE 1 OF 7
Foundation Translation Routine
Why Are We Doing This?

The Translation + CLIR Drills in this Routine are the foundation of your entire LSAT prep journey. This is the most important homework you will do during your LSAT prep training, even compared to PTs.

This Routine builds a foundation in LR Translation before we port your Translation skills over to RC in the next Routine.

LR
RC
Frequency
Daily Foundation
Challenge Index
Pretty Chill
Level
Beginner
Study block
2-4 hours
Time goal to move on
20 min
Routine Schedule

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

1
Translation + CLIR Drill
≥ 3 SECTIONS
2
Extracurricular Reading
3
Vocab Training
Once A Week, Do This Instead
1
Translation Marathon
8 SECTIONS
≥ 1X PER WEEK
How To Pull This Off

Your progression toward the Translation time and accuracy goals is primarily determined by two things: volume and following the instructions.

To maximize your progress in this Routine, do all your Translation + CLIR Drills consecutively; do not take breaks between Translation + CLIR Drills. Do not review your Translation + CLIR Drills in between sections. All review should be done in a separate sitting.

Do at least 3 consecutive Translation + CLIR Drills per day, if possible. Ideally, you would complete 6 Translation + CLIR drills consecutively per day. Doing 1 Translation + CLIR Drill per day will not improve your skills; it will keep your skills the same. You will only start improving on your second consecutive Translation + CLIR Drill; this is why it is so useful to do at least 3 consecutive Translation + CLIR Drills every day.

Add a Translation Marathon to your Daily Practice at least once per week. If you can manage to do Translation + CLIR Marathons more often, you will progress to the time goal faster.

Extracurricular Reading and Vocab should always be done at the end of your Routine to gradually expand your common sense in the subject areas where you're weakest. If you struggle with science passages, emphasize daily science engagement in the Extracurricular Reading. If you struggle with abstract language, emphasize daily humanities engagement in the Extracurricular Reading.

How To Move On

Once you are halfway to your Translation + CLIR Drill time goal, move to the next Routine: Translation + Decaf.

The time goal for Translation + CLIR Drills is 20 minutes. The accommodated time goals for Translation + CLIR Drills are 25 minutes for 53-minute accommodations and 30 minutes for 70-minute accommodations. Meeting this Translation + CLIR Drill time goal is only valid under two conditions: you have a CLIR for every stimulus and you have translated and quipped every stimulus in the section out loud. Ideally, you should hit -5 accuracy against the CLIR Answer Key consistently in order to beat the time goal, but this accuracy goal may be adjusted according to your score goals.

Example of When to Move On: You started at 52 minutes per out loud Translation + CLIR Drill section and you don't have accommodations, so your time goal is 20 minutes. The midpoint of 52 and 20 is 36, so you would move on when your time hits 36 minutes.

I got halfway to my Translation + CLIR time goal! 🎉

OBJECTIVE 1 OF 7
Create a Realistic Prep Plan and Study Schedule
What Problem Are We Solving?

The single biggest problem in LSAT prep is unrealistic planning and timelines. You absolutely can train yourself to massively improve your logic and Translation skills. But ya'll randomly pick test dates that make it impossible to train your skills in the amount of time you have before the test. This leads to panic, LSAT scores that shock and demotivate you, and an altogether toxic relationship with the test.

How You Know You Need To Do This
Is This Worth My Time?

You don't prioritize LSAT prep in your calendar and will consistently skip studying whenever anything else comes up
You don't block your study time on Google Calendar
You just picked your test date because it was the next one and you want to get this over with

What Problem Are We Solving?

If you don't know the process, you're taking on way more burden for figuring out how to beat this exam than you have to. Not learning the strategies for each RC question type leaves you alone responsible for figuring out the best way to do it, on-the-fly and in the middle of a section.
